summary: For 9–10 year olds: solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (e.g. a recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → cost of 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2). The through-line is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by a double number line, ratio table and bar model. Learners should experience scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with the common additive 'add the difference' error, across authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes). Activities range from a manipulable double-number-line scaler that builds the proportional feel, through a Socratic unit-rate dialogue, a worked annotated exemplar, to checkable practice with targeted distractors.
misconceptions: Scaling additively — adding the difference in people/kg instead of multiplying by the ratio (recipe for 6 = recipe for 4 + 2 portions of everything, done wrongly).
Not finding the unit value, so unable to scale to a new amount.
Inverting the rate (£12 per 3 kg treated as £3 per kg).
Confusing scaling up with down, or mis-applying ×1/2.
Treating rate problems as unrelated to multiplicative comparison / fractions.

activities.title: Double-number-line scaler: find one unit, then scale
steps: On two parallel lines locked by a rate (e.g. kilograms against cost in pounds, £), slide to mark 3 kg opposite £12.
Use a 'find 1 unit' action to collapse the lines to 1 kg = £4, then slide on to 5 kg and read off £20.
Switch to a recipe mode: scale ingredients by ×6/4 (e.g. 200 g flour for 4 people → how much for 6?) shown on a bar model.
Switch to a shape mode: halve every dimension (×1/2) and read the new measurements.

Try the 'additive trap' toggle: add the same number to both lines (3 kg + 2 = 5 kg, so £12 + 2 = £14), then compare with the locked-rate result of £20. Notice that adding matching amounts instead (2 kg and its value, £8) keeps the lines aligned and gives £20.
activities.insight: Scaling and rates are proportional, multiplicative relationships: finding the value of one unit unlocks any target amount, and adding the same difference to both quantities does not preserve the relationship.

activities.title: Unit-rate dialogue: 'what does one cost?'
steps: Respond to a market-trader or chef character posing rate and recipe problems: 'If 3 kg costs £12, what does ONE kilogram cost? So what about five?'
State the unit value aloud or in writing, then state how you scale it to the target amount.
Answer the probe 'Someone said 6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more — what's wrong with that?' and explain the flaw.
Tackle a stretch case ('a recipe for 4, but you need it for 10') and say whether the unit-value method still works.
activities.insight: Routing every proportional problem through 'the value of one, then times the target' is a reliable general habit that works even when the scale factor is not a whole number.

activities.title: Worked exemplar: annotated double number line and ratio table
steps: Study an annotated double number line (kg vs £) and a ratio table with a unit-value column.
Reveal the unitary steps one at a time: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = £4 → 5 kg = £20.
Read the ratio table to see the unit column (1 person = 50 g) and how scaled values follow from it.
Use the exemplar as a reference, then solve a new, different rate/scaling problem yourself.
activities.insight: The unit value is the key column of a ratio table / anchor point of a double number line; scaled values are multiples of it.

activities.title: Checkable practice with additive-error distractors
steps: Fill in the unitary steps: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = □ → 5 kg = □.
Choose the correct recipe-for-6 amount from options that include an additive distractor (e.g. 400 g from 'add 200 g for 2 more people' vs the correct 300 g).
Select the correct multiplier for a scaling problem (e.g. ×6/4 = ×1.5, ×1/2).
Use a slider to set the scaled quantity and check it against the unit value.
activities.insight: Correct proportional answers come from multiplying the unit value or applying the right fractional multiplier; additive answers are identifiable errors.

checkQuestion: Give the child rate/scaling problems to solve, watching their method: 'A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?' and 'If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?' Watch whether they find a unit value or a scale factor, or whether they just add on a difference.
checkAnswer: Flour: 300 g (200 ÷ 4 = 50 g per person, × 6 = 300; or scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200 × 1.5). Cost: £20 (£12 ÷ 3 = £4 per kg, × 5 = £20). The teacher watches for a multiplicative route — unit rate or scale factor — not additive 'add 2 more people so add 200 g'.
